USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Let the already-announced July 6 List 1 tariffs (25% on ~$34B) take effect and otherwise hold. Do not trigger the additional ~$200B/10% list tomorrow, and do not roll back List 1 or revive a May-style purchase-only truce. Keep a negotiating channel open for structural IP and tech-transfer remedies, treating List 2 (~$16B) and the $200B identification as contingent leverage rather than an immediate next shot.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is only slightly above neutral. The U.S. still has the stronger 301 case and the more asymmetric goods relationship, and the domestic macro is not yet showing a trade-war recession: industrial production is up, consumer sentiment remains near 98, and VIX is ~16 rather than crisis-level. The $34B list was deliberately aimed at industrial/tech lines, not consumer staples, and Barclays-type estimates circulating in mid-June put a $50B package at about 0.1pp of GDP. That is not a +0.5 “material GDP drag” event. What keeps the reading from turning into an opportunity is that China has already matched dollar-for-dollar and aimed the reply at soybeans, autos, and other politically salient U.S. exports: China takes ~60% of U.S. soybean exports (~$14B), futures have fallen ~$1.50/bu since late May (~$6B paper loss on the 2018 crop), and the May 19 joint statement / Mnuchin “on hold” truce collapsed within ten days when Washington proceeded with 301. June 3 Beijing talks then ended with China refusing extra purchases unless tariffs were taken off the table. Firing the $200B list now would convert a still-manageable opening salvo into a cascade China has already said it will answer with “quantity and quality” measures, while walking List 1 back on the eve of implementation would spend the 301 finding for nothing after ZTE was already given a lifeline. Hold the announced posture, watch whether List 1 plus yuan weakness (CNY near 6.64–6.72) and China’s export dependence produce a real negotiating opening, and keep the larger lists in reserve.
key_factors: List 1 25% on ~$34B is scheduled for July 6; China has already announced matching 25% on U.S. soy, autos, seafood, and related lines the same day
Trump directed USTR on June 18 to identify an extra ~$200B at 10% if China retaliates; that list is a threat, not yet in force
May 19 purchase-increase truce collapsed by May 29; June 3 Ross-Liu talks ended in impasse
U.S. real economy still firm (IP up, sentiment ~97.9, VIX ~16); goods deficit and China imports have not yet compressed
CNY has weakened into the mid-6.6s, a partial Chinese offset and a stress signal, not a U.S. financial-stability event
Soy/farm-belt exposure is the main U.S. vulnerability (~$14B, ~1/3 of the U.S. crop) and is already showing up in futures
ZTE denial-order leverage was already spent in early June for a fine/monitor/management deal; further non-tariff gifts are not warranted
A measured hold preserves 301 credibility without immediately climbing the $200B/$450B ladder that would pull in consumer goods and invite broader market and ally blowback

Barclays cited mid-June: $50B tariffs ~0.1pp hit at most to annual U.S. growth and a similar CPI bump — small relative to an $18T economy.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Implement tomorrow the already-announced matching 25 percent tariffs on the first $34 billion of U.S. goods (soybeans, autos, aquatic products) and keep the second $16 billion tranche aligned with the U.S. List 2 calendar. Do not add new tariff lines, entity-style measures, or a directed yuan devaluation beyond that proportionate mirror. Keep a negotiation channel open, but offer no fresh purchase or structural commitments until Washington actually suspends Section 301.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material and rising, not existential. USTR’s two-stage $50 billion plan (List 1, ~$34 billion / 818 lines, effective 6 July; List 2 ~$16 billion later) is aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and other industrially significant technologies—i.e., the Made in China 2025 stack—and Trump on 18 June directed a further ~$200 billion at 10 percent if China answers the $50 billion action. The April ZTE denial order showed that U.S. component bans can idle a national champion; Congress is already widening the aperture to Huawei. That is a real hit to export-tech interests and to the credibility of industrial policy, which is why the score is well above zero. It is not +0.5: Chinese industrial production is still +6.0 percent y/y, CPI is tame, the discount rate is unchanged at 2.9 percent, and reserves remain ~$3.14 trillion. The yuan has weakened sharply (DEXCHUS 6.64 on 3 July vs ~6.40 in mid-June; monthly EXCHUS 6.72 vs 6.32 in February), but Yi Gang/Pan Gongsheng have already moved to cap a disorderly slide rather than run a currency war. Action should be retaliate, not a wider escalate: China already nullified the 19 May purchase-truce after the White House resumed 301 on 29 May, so walking back the 15 June matching list the day before implementation would reward U.S. bad faith and look like unilateral concession. A dollar-for-dollar farm/auto mirror is the minimum that preserves deterrence and exploits U.S. political exposure (China takes ~$14 billion of U.S. soybeans). Going beyond that match, or treating the yuan as a weapon, would make the threatened $200 billion list more likely and convert a contained first tranche into a much larger export shock. Hold the second-order line: match what is already on the table, do not feed the next escalation.
key_factors: U.S. List 1 25% on ~$34B Chinese tech/industrial goods effective 6 July; List 2 ~$16B pending
Trump 18 June directive to identify ~$200B more at 10% if China retaliates

CNY depreciation and PBOC verbal intervention: FX pressure is a warning, not a crisis
China IP still +6% y/y, reserves ~$3.14T, CPI stable — real-economy bite still prospective
